payload.objective: Audit inherited taxonomies of thought: is a taxonomy a structure already present in the texts (discovered) or a label imposed later (invented)? Use two leak-free designs: a sealed text (Mawangdui manuscript, buried 168 BCE) and a sealed reader (a language model trained only on pre-1931 text).

H-C1.claim: The six-schools taxonomy predicts where an unseen book falls better than era, region or genre taxonomies.
H-C1.decision: rank by chance-corrected score with 95% bootstrap interval; require agreement across instruments (lex, lex_tr) for a main claim

H-C2.claim: The instrument ranks chapters that scholars regard as Daoist-leaning (Guanzi: Neiye, Xinshu I-II, Baixin; Han Feizi: Jie Lao, Yu Lao) high on Daoist affinity within their own books.
H-C2.decision: PASS if mean target percentile >= 80 and permutation p < 0.05; otherwise the instrument fails validation and no main conclusion may be published

H-C3.claim: The sealed manuscript sits between Dao and Fa instead of falling cleanly into one school.
H-C3.decision: 'constructed' prediction holds if dominant label share < 0.70 OR mean margin below the 10th percentile of transmitted books; otherwise the 'real structure' prediction holds

H-W1.claim: A reader sealed in 1930 already separates what was later called analytic vs continental philosophy.

H-W2.claim: A modern reader separates the later label more sharply than the 1930 reader, beyond its general advantage on labels that already existed in 1930 (hindsight gap G > 0).

decision_rules_after_first_tournament: If the six-schools taxonomy leads AND the tomb test supports 'real structure': next experiment = extend the sealed-text test to the Guodian slips.

If the six-schools taxonomy leads BUT the tomb test supports 'constructed': rewrite the conclusion as 'school structure holds in Han-edited transmitted books but not out of sample'; prioritise the translation-arm rerun.
If an era, region or genre taxonomy leads: reopen the premise that the school is the basic unit; next experiment = school test within era strata.

payload.title: Sima Tan's six schools (Lun liujia yaozhi, Shiji 130): Yin-Yang, Confucian, Mohist, Names, Legalist, Daoist
payload.source_claim: Six-fold partition of the early Chinese masters proposed by Sima Tan (Grand Astrologer, d. 110 BCE) in his essay 'Lun liujia yaozhi' (論六家要旨), preserved in Shiji ch. 130 (Taishigong zixu), completed by his son Sima Qian ca. 91 BCE; Tan's essay names yinyang jia, ru jia, mo jia, ming jia, fa jia and dao jia (documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sima_Tan and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Schools_of_Thought). This taxonomy transfers Tan's six labels onto the 23 transmitted books of the corpus, following the Han bibliographic tradition (Hanshu Yiwenzhi; context in Hunter 2019, https://doi.org/10.7817/jameroriesoci.138.4.0763) and standard sinological reference works. Books that Han bibliography placed in categories OUTSIDE the six schools (military/bing, ritual canon, Zajia eclectics, Zongheng diplomacy) are force-assigned to the least-bad class and marked contested; the Yin-Yang class receives no book because its central figure Zou Yan's writings are all lost (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zou_Yan).

payload.claim: T_six formalizes Sima Tan's six-school partition (Lun liujia yaozhi, Shiji 130, ca. 100 BCE; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sima_Tan) over the 23 transmitted books. Partition: Confucian 8 (Analects, Mencius, Xunzi, Liji*, Xiaojing, Kongzi_Jiayu, Zhongyong, Sima_Fa*), Daoist 9 (Laozi, Zhuangzi, Liezi*, Guanzi*, Lushi_Chunqiu*, Huainanzi*, Guiguzi*, Sunzi_Bingfa*, Liutao*), Legalist 4 (Han_Feizi, Shangjunshu, Wuzi*, Wei_Liaozi*), Mohist 1 (Mozi), Names 1 (Gongsun_Longzi), Yin-Yang 0. * = contested (11 units total).
key_findings: Yin-Yang class is necessarily EMPTY: its central figure Zou Yan's writings are all lost (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zou_Yan); no transmitted book in this corpus is a yin-yang school text. The six-schools partition cannot fill one of its own classes from the transmitted corpus.

Five books (Sunzi_Bingfa, Wuzi, Liutao, Sima_Fa, Wei_Liaozi) are Seven Military Classics texts that Han bibliography filed in the bing (military) category, outside the six schools; all are contested force-assignments.
Guanzi: Hanshu Yiwenzhi = Daoist, Suishu = Legalist, modern = syncretic Jixia composite (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/管子_(書)); assigned Daoist per the earliest Han classification.

Lushi_Chunqiu and Huainanzi were both Zajia (Syncretist) in Han bibliography; both assigned Daoist (Huang-Lao reading) per modern scholarship (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huainanzi; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/呂氏春秋), noting the Siku quanshu read Lushi_Chunqiu as Confucian-dominant.

Liutao is the ONLY unit with citation 'uncertain': its Taigong corpus is traditionally placed in the Yiwenzhi Daoist category, but no citable URL was retrievable from the lab tools; assignment documented as least-bad, not source-backed.

payload.claim: Sima Tan (c. 165-110 BCE), Grand Astrologer under Emperor Wu of Han, is the traditional author of the essay 'Lun liujia yaozhi' (Essential Meanings of the Six Schools), preserved as part of Shiji ch. 130 (Taishigong zixu), the autobiographical postface of Sima Qian's Shiji (composed late 2nd-early 1st c. BCE, building on Sima Tan's drafts; Tan died 110 BCE). The essay evaluates six kinds of governance/scholarly traditions using 'jia' (family/expert) labels: Yinyangjia (Naturalists, central figure Zou Yan), Rujia (Confucians), Mojia (Mohists), Mingjia (School of Names), Fajia (Legalists), and Daojia (Dao school). Per Kidder Smith (2003), Daojia — and likewise 'Legalism' (Fajia) — are Sima Tan's retrospective coinages: the essay invents these categories to group heterogeneous thinkers, and is primarily an argument FOR the Daojia (a wuwei-centered, Huang-Lao-inflected statecraft) against the shortcomings of the other five.
contested: Date of composition: no independent attestation. Standard accounts place it late in Tan's life (he died 110 BCE, the year of the fengshan sacrifice from which he was excluded — the Shiji frames the essay near his death); Kidder Smith treats it as an early-Wu-reign text and his 2003 article is the standard re-examination of its date, authorship and intent. Preregistered dating for our purposes: between 141 BCE (Wu accession) and 110 BCE (Tan's death).

Whether the jia categories were 'invented' by Tan or reported existing discourse: Smith (2003) argues invention (esp. Daojia/Fajia/Mingjia as new labels); the Huang-Lao wiki synthesis notes Tan likely coined Daojia with existing Huang-Lao literature in mind; Lee (2014) shows 'Ru-Mo' pairings in pre-imperial texts may not map onto the received 'Confucian/Mohist schools' reading — i.e., at least Ru and Mo have some pre-imperial attestation as designations, while the sixfold scheme as a system is Han.

Whether Tan's 'jia' meant 'school' at all: Wikipedia's Sima Tan article stresses 'jia' could mean 'expert' or 'family'; it likely did not occur to Tan that the categories would be used as historical schools with memberships.

payload.claim: The Hanshu Yiwenzhi ('Treatise on Literature', Hanshu ch. 30, compiled by Ban Gu (32-92 CE); Hanshu finished 111 CE) is the earliest extant imperial bibliography. It derives from Liu Xin's Qilue ('Seven Summaries', late Western Han), itself based on Liu Xiang's Bielu ('Abstracts'). Its Zhuzi lue section defines the 'nine streams, ten schools' (jiuliu shijia): Rujia, Daojia, Yinyangjia, Fajia, Mingjia, Mojia, Zonghengjia, Zajia, Nongjia — plus Xiaoshuojia ('fiction'), making ten schools of which nine are counted as streams. Relation to Sima Tan: it retains all six of Tan's school-names verbatim and ADDS Zonghengjia (diplomatists), Zajia (eclectics) and Nongjia (agriculturalists), and it situates the masters within a larger six-division catalogue of ALL literature (Liuyi/classics, Zhuzi, Shifu/poetry, Bingshu/military, Shushu/numerology, Fangji/techniques). Key difference from Tan's essay: the Yiwenzhi is a library catalogue of books with authorship/title entries, not an evaluative essay on doctrines; its classifications are bibliographic placements, and it postdates Tan by roughly 150-200 years (based on Liu Xiang/Liu Xin's late-1st-c.-BCE collation). The frozen rival taxonomy T_yiwenzhi_nine (r0008) formalizes exactly this scheme.
contested: Emic status: Csikszentmihalyi & Nylan (2003) treat both the six-school and nine-stream schemes as constructed lineages invented by Han authors; Lee (2014) shows the pre-imperial 'Ru-Mo' usage may not mean 'Confucians and Mohists' as schools; against this, the categories' partial pre-imperial attestation (Ru, Mo, and discourse about 'the ways of the daode' in Zhuangzi/Xunzi/Tianxia) gives the rival position that Han cataloguers were formalizing existing self- and other-designations, not inventing from nothing.

The nine-streams taxonomy's own internal logic (each school 'flowing from' a classical office/kingly institution) is a Ban Gu/Liu Xin ideological framing, and modern scholars disagree on how much weight to give it as evidence of intellectual structure (see He 2024 for the classification-systems literature; Hunter 2019 JAOS for the Yiwenzhi's construction).

Which texts fall in which stream is itself a Han judgement that later catalogues reversed (see item 6, Guanzi: Daojia in Hanshu, Fajia in Suishu) — evidence that stream-assignments were classification decisions, not discovered essences.
sources: https://doi.org/10.62051/jhf9wg08 (Qiaoxuan He 2024, 'Cataloging and the study of ancient Chinese book classification systems'; URL verified)
https://doi.org/10.7817/jameroriesoci.138.4.0763 (Michael Hunter, JAOS 138.4 (2019) — Han bibliography context, as cited in r0004/r0008)

payload.claim: In 26 BCE Emperor Cheng commissioned Liu Xiang (77-6 BCE) to collate the Han imperial library; over ~20 years Liu Xiang's team compared duplicate manuscripts of each work, eliminated redundancies, fixed chapter order and titles, and wrote a memorial/preface (xulu) per book, producing the Bielu; his son Liu Xin completed the project and produced the Qilue, the basis of the Hanshu Yiwenzhi. Most transmitted masters texts exist in forms mediated by this collation — e.g., the received Guanzi was edited by Liu Xiang c. 26 BCE; Liu Xiang also edited Zhanguoce, Shuoyuan, Xinxu, and the Xunzi-type compilations. Implications for 'discovered vs invented' tests on the 23 transmitted books: (a) any corpus-wide statistical signal (style normalization, chapterization, lexical standardization) may partly reflect Han editorial conventions shared ACROSS schools, which would inflate apparent within-school coherence or create corpus-wide artifacts; (b) excavated manuscripts sealed before/independent of the collation (Mawangdui 168 BCE; also Guodian c. 300 BCE, Yinqueshan 168 BCE) serve as the correct control condition, since they preserve pre-collation text states; (c) conversely, collation selected among and combined pre-existing manuscript lineages rather than inventing texts ex nihilo, so transmitted books still carry Warring States material.
contested: Degree of Han editorial intervention: Pines (2016) shows the received Book of Lord Shang is a Western Han (Liu Xiang-era) compilation whose received shape tells us little about pre-imperial authorship; Krijgsman (2016) and Hanmo Zhang (2018) document a fluid manuscript culture in early China (variants, accretion, collective text-making, no fixed 'original'), against older views of the collation as light-touch copy-editing of stable books.

What the collation implies for school labels: one position (Csikszentmihalyi & Nylan 2003; Smith 2003) holds that because the library project itself was organized by the Liu Xin/Ban Gu categories, the transmitted corpus came down to us pre-sorted by a Han taxonomy — circularity risk for any test that validates school labels using transmitted texts alone. The rival position holds that excavated texts (Mawangdui, Guodian, Yinqueshan, Tsinghua/Shanghai Museum bamboo) largely confirm the pre-imperial existence of the textual traditions the catalogues describe, so the collation fixed rather than fabricated lineages.

payload.claim: Kidder Smith, 'Sima Tan and the Invention of Daoism, "Legalism," et cetera' (Journal of Asian Studies 62.1, 2003, pp. 129-156; 90+ citations) argues that Sima Tan's essay invented the category Daojia (and, as the title's scare-quotes indicate, 'Fajia' and the other jia): the six-fold scheme is a single Han author's retrospective construction that groups heterogeneous thinkers under new labels, chiefly to argue FOR a Daojia-style (wuwei-centered) statecraft; reading these jia as self-aware Warring States schools with memberships and doctrines is anachronistic, and 'Daoism' as a named entity begins with this essay. Csikszentmihalyi & Nylan, 'Constructing Lineages and Inventing Traditions through Exemplary Figures in Early China' (T'oung Pao 89, 2003, pp. 59-99; 110+ citations) argue that early-Chinese authors constructed intellectual lineages and invented traditions through exemplary figures (master-disciple chains, sage genealogies, apocryphal encounters such as Confucius meeting Laozi); the 'schools' of the received taxonomy are products of this lineage-construction practice, projected backwards, not reports of contemporaneous intellectual communities. Both works are the standard citations for the CONSTRUCTEDNESS side of our audit question, and both are directly relevant: they predict that a six-schools structure imposed on the corpus is an etic Han frame rather than emic Warring States structure.
contested: Rival position 1 (emic core): Lee (2014) shows 'Ru' and 'Mo' were in pre-imperial use as designations (though 'Ru-Mo' may not mean 'Confucians and Mohists' as schools); Mengzi/Mozi/Zhuangzi attest self-conscious Ru and Mo communities, so parts of the taxonomy have pre-imperial grounding — the dispute is over WHICH categories are emic (plausibly Ru, Mo; maybe 'daode' discourse) vs etic (Daojia, Fajia, Mingjia, Yinyangjia as unified schools).

Rival position 2 (real Huang-Lao): much Chinese scholarship treats Huang-Lao (the content behind Tan's Daojia) as a genuine, identifiable Warring States-to-early-Han current; Michael (2023, Religions) surveys this 'fiercely debated' divide between Western skeptics and Chinese proponents. Van Ess's analysis of Shiji/Hanshu biographies (summarized at Huang-Lao wiki) found the 'Huang-Lao' label attached to identifiable persons/factions in early Han — a middle position: the label designated something real in Han usage even if the six-school scheme is retrojective.

Even Smith accepts the essay is genuinely Sima Tan's and historically situated (early Wu reign); the invention claim is about the CATEGORIES, not the authorship. No major published position denies the essay's existence/attribution, though exact dating remains unsettled (see item 1).

payload.claim: Mawangdui (Changsha, Hunan; tombs of the Changsha Kingdom, Western Han) tomb 3 — excavated December 1973, site excavated 1972-1974 — was sealed in 168 BCE; its occupant was a male believed to be the son of Chancellor Li Cang (tomb 2) and Xin Zhui/Lady Dai (tomb 1). Tomb 3 yielded ~28 silk manuscripts (Mawangdui boshu, ~120,000 characters) including two Laozi copies (A, small-seal script, earlier; B, clerical script, later) with the DE chapters preceding the DAO chapters, plus four previously unknown texts prefixed to Laozi B. In 1974-75 Tang Lan identified these four texts (Jingfa, Shiliu jing [Jing], Cheng, Yuandao) as the lost 'Huangdi Sijing' (Yellow Emperor's Four Classics) listed in the Hanshu Yiwenzhi under Daojia (Huangdi sijing, 4 pian); the label 'Huang-Lao boshu' (Huang-Lao silk texts) is widely used. The 168 BCE sealing gives a hard terminus ante quem for the manuscripts; the burial-date control for our tomb_test is therefore solid.
contested: IDENTITY: most scholars accept Tang Lan's Huangdi Sijing identification, but some reject or suspend it, preferring neutral labels 'Huang-Lao boshu' or 'Huangdi shu' (Wikipedia Huangdi Sijing records both positions). Our sealed unit should therefore be labeled provisionally, not as established fact.

COMPOSITION DATE: the four texts' composition is dated anywhere from mid-Warring States (4th c. BCE, Tang Lan's view) to late Warring States/Qin or even early Han; manuscript copying predates 168 BCE (Laozi B avoids the bang-taboo and is usually dated c. 206-180 BCE; A is earlier still in seal script). The gap between composition and burial is itself disputed.

HUANG-LAO QUESTION: whether 'Huang-Lao' names a coherent school is contested — Michael (2023) surveys the Western-skeptic vs Chinese-proponent divide; van Ess found the Shiji/Hanshu 'Huang-Lao' label marking identifiable persons/factions rather than a doctrinal school; the Wikipedia Huang-Lao article notes Daojia and Huang-Lao are used interchangeably in the Shiji though they are not identical. For the audit: the sealed manuscript is a test case precisely because no received catalogue ever sorted it — if our instrument assigns it a school, that is an out-of-sample prediction, not a lookup.

payload.claim: The Guanzi (received form: 76 of 86 chapters surviving; >135,000 characters; edited/compiled by Liu Xiang c. 26 BCE) was classified DIFFERENTLY across the major catalogues: the Hanshu Yiwenzhi lists it under DAOJIA (Daoists); the Suishu Jingjizhi (636 CE) moved it to FAJIA (Legalists); and the Qing Siku Quanshu places it in the zibu FAJIA lei (Legalist class) — zh Wikipedia states explicitly: Hanshu Yiwenzhi列入道家類, Suishu Jingjizhi改列法家類, Siku Quanshu為子部法家類. The text is today regarded as a multi-author, multi-century composite associated with the Jixia Academy at Linzi (Qi), with much content of late-Warring-States date; the Han Feizi is the earliest work referencing 'Guanzi'-type material (proto-Guanzi possibly taking shape c. 250 BCE). For our audit this is a canonical case that school labels are catalogue DECISIONS that changed across dynasties for the same book, not discovered properties of the text.
contested: Which catalogue got it 'right' is not a settled question — modern scholarship (e.g., Rickett's translation; Sato Masayuki) treats the Guanzi as syncretic; the en-Wikipedia article notes Sato disagrees with Rickett's dating of some chapters to the Han, agreeing instead on a late-Warring-States date for most of the work.

Chapter-level attributions: Guo Moruo held Xinshu shang/xia, Baixin and Neiye to be works of Song Xing and Yin Wen (a pair filed under MOJIA in the Hanshu Yiwenzhi) — meaning the same chapters our defectors target have been claimed for Daoist (Roth), Huang-Lao/Legalist-syncretic (Rickett), and Mohist-adjacent (Guo Moruo) traditions; Xu Kangsheng likewise judged the Xinshu/Neiye chapters as 'attached to the Daoists' (附會道家) rather than genuinely Guan Zhong-era.

The Suishu reclassification's motivation (Qing/Sui scholars emphasizing the text's fajia statecraft vs the Han reading emphasizing its Huang-Lao/Daoist content) is standard but rests on catalogue evidence, not on a stated rationale in the catalogues themselves.

payload.claim: Scholarly basis for the pre-registered defector chapters. GUANZI Neiye/Xinshu I (shang)/Xinshu II (xia)/Baixin: the Neiye (c. 350 BCE per the received-text literature) is called by A. C. Graham 'possibly the oldest mystical text in China'; Harold D. Roth (Original Tao, 1999) describes it as 'a manual on the theory and practice of meditation that contains the earliest references to breath control and the earliest discussion of the physiological basis of self-cultivation in the Chinese tradition', and perhaps the oldest extant text of Daoism; it was re-evaluated in the 20th century as a 'proto-Daoist' text that influenced the Daodejing and Zhuangzi, with the first references to cultivating jing/qi/shen (later core Daoist-neidan vocabulary). Xinshu shang/xia and Baixin are conventionally treated as later works in the same inner-cultivation lineage (Xinshu I partially reworking Neiye material). HAN FEIZI Jie Lao (ch. 20) and Yu Lao (ch. 21): the Han Feizi 'is believed to contain the first commentaries on the Dao De Jing' — the two chapters quote and gloss Laozi passages (analysed and translated in Queen 2012). The Daoist-leaning characterization is thus based on: meditation/qi-cultivation content (Guanzi four), direct Laozi quotation and exegesis (Han Feizi two).
contested: The 'Daoist' label on the Guanzi four is contested, not consensus: (a) Roth's proto-Daoist reading is the dominant Western position, but (b) Guo Moruo attributed Xinshu shang/xia, Baixin and Neiye to Song Xing and Yin Wen — figures whose book (Songzi) is filed under MOJIA in the Hanshu Yiwenzhi; (c) Xu Kangsheng judged these chapters later Daoist accretions ('附會道家') into a largely Legalist-colored book; (d) the Guanzi as a whole moved Daojia→Fajia across catalogues (item 6). So the four chapters are defectors from a Legalist-filed BOOK toward Daoist content — exactly the instrument-validation logic intended — but the direction is only as secure as Roth's lineage reading.

Jie Lao/Yu Lao: en-Wikipedia notes the two Laozi-commentary chapters 'have generally been considered addendums due to considerable ideological, lexical, and stylistic differences' from the rest of the Han Feizi — their authenticity as Han Fei's own work is disputed; whether they represent 'Legalist appropriation of Laozi' vs 'Huang-Lao syncretism' vs a distinct commentator is debated (Queen 2012; Harris 2026 on the Han Feizi's dissection of the Laozi). The Han Feizi itself is THE canonical Fajia text (Hanshu Yiwenzhi Fajia; 'culminating Legalist text'), so these two chapters are defectors from a Legalist-classified book toward Laozi commentary.

General caveat: 'Daoist-leaning' is a modern analytic label applied to content (inner cultivation, Laozi exegesis, wuwei, qi/jing/shen vocabulary); none of these chapters self-identifies as Daojia — the category did not exist until Sima Tan (items 1, 4). Defector performance should be interpreted accordingly.

payload.verdict_on_H-C2: PASS is technically met but not construct-validating as reported; at least four trivial-pass routes remain unexcluded
attacks: (1) Quotation leakage: Jie Lao/Yu Lao are Laozi commentaries containing extended verbatim Laozi quotations; if the Daoist centroid includes Laozi, high affinity is guaranteed by shared strings, not doctrinal signal.

(2) Register/meter confound: Neiye and Baixin are rhymed verse; Laozi is the only verse_aphorisms book in the corpus. The Han Feizi top5 (Shuonan, Yangquan, Zhudao — all abstract/aphoristic/rhetorical chapters — outranking Jie Lao) and Guanzi top5 (Shuidi, a verse chapter, in 3rd) are direct evidence the score tracks 'abstract/verse philosophical register', not Daoist content specifically. No discriminant validity check (targets' percentiles under OTHER class centroids) was reported.

(3) Non-independence + circular target definition: the 4 Guanzi targets are one genetic Huang-Lao cluster, not 4 units; effective n is ~2 books. Worse, 'Daoist-leaning' defector chapters were identified by a scholarly tradition descending from the Han catalog that also produced T_six (r0021: Kidder Smith — Daojia is Tan's retrospective coinage), so H-C2 partly validates 'lex recovers Han catalog judgments' — the very thing under test.

(4) Centroid self-inclusion: Guanzi is itself labeled Daoist in T_six; if Guanzi contributed to the Daoist centroid, within-Guanzi targets self-match. Permutation p = 1e-4 appears to be the resolution floor (0/9999), and within-book chapter permutation assumes exchangeability the target cluster violates.
tournament_confounders: Class-structure asymmetry: T_six = 5 non-empty classes, Daoist catch-all 9/23 (39%, >=6 least-bad force-fits), singletons Mozi & Gongsun Longzi, EMPTY Yinyang class. T_yiwenzhi_nine = 9 classes, max 5/23, singletons Mingjia/Zonghengjia/Mojia, doubles Fajia/Zajia. T_lit = 5 classes, singletons Laozi(verse) & Guiguzi(rhetoric). T_era = 5 strata. Raw and even chance-corrected scores are not comparable without pre-registering a correction validated against per-taxonomy permutation nulls.

Record error: r0014/prompt say T_era has ONE singleton class; the frozen labels show TWO (Sunzi_Bingfa alone in Early SA/eWS; Liezi alone in Post-Han). Singleton units are near-guaranteed LOUO misses (no same-class training exemplar), penalizing each taxonomy by a different fixed amount.

Label-noise asymmetry: contested = 11/23 (T_six), 8/23 (T_lit), 14/23 (T_era), 5/23 (T_yiwenzhi). T_yiwenzhi labels are catalog facts; T_era labels are modern datings. A T_yiwenzhi win could be pure label-reliability attenuation of rivals, not discovered structure.

drop_contested=True yields NON-COMPARABLE subcorpora: T_six->12 books, T_lit->15, T_era->9, T_yiwenzhi->18; for T_era it deletes most of the military cluster (Sunzi, Wuzi, Wei_Liaozi, Liutao contested) i.e. the strongest lexical axis (corpus_map dim1). Books uncontested in ALL four taxonomies = {Gongsun_Longzi, Xunzi} only, so a matched joint subset is impossible.

Taxonomies are not independent tests: T_six and T_yiwenzhi share 6 class names and most assignments; both encode Han catalog structure. Interpretation must be pre-registered: T_yiwenzhi >= T_six is NOT evidence against Sima Tan (same historical source of structure); only T_era/T_lit > T_six is.

Military-axis dominance: the cleanest lexical split in the corpus is military vs rest. T_yiwenzhi has a real Bingshu class; T_six force-fits military books into Daoist/Legalist/Confucian; T_lit splits them across treatises/dialogues. The tournament may mostly measure 'does the taxonomy respect the bing axis'.

payload.claim: Prior computational studies relevant to pre-Qin/Han corpora. Verified examples: (1) Wu & Wang 2025, 'Quantitative analysis of semantic boundaries in four ancient Chinese philosophies' (npj Heritage Science) — quantitative measurement of the semantic boundaries between four received philosophical traditions (Confucian/Daoist/Legalist/Mohist lineage texts); the closest published analogue to our core question: it probes whether the received school categories correspond to detectable lexical-semantic clusters. (2) Wu & Wang 2024, 'Tracing the evolution of ancient Chinese military science through classical texts' (Heritage Science) — quantitative text analysis of the military-text tradition (relevant to our bingshu-filed contested books). (3) Duan, Wang, Yang & Su 2023, 'Disentangling the cultural evolution of ancient China: a digital humanities perspective' (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 18+ citations) — models cultural/intellectual evolution across ancient Chinese texts with DH methods. (4) McManus, Li, Tam & Qiu 2025, 'Measuring accommodation: a quantitative text-reuse analysis of Matteo Ricci's reliance on Chinese classics' (Int. J. Digital Humanities) — text-reuse detection methodology applied to the Chinese classics (the citation/parallel-detection toolkit our 'defector' logic resembles). Qualitative-but-load-bearing background: Krijgsman 2016 and Hanmo Zhang 2018 (manuscript culture / text-making) caution against treating units as fixed books. Known gap: supervised 'school classification' or stylometric authorship attribution of the early masters corpus is sparse in the indexed literature compared with later Chinese vernacular fiction (e.g., Hongloumeng attribution debates); we found NO prior study doing exactly what the preregistration does (six-schools vs nine-streams vs form/era tournaments + sealed-manuscript out-of-sample test).
contested: Methodological caution found in the literature and applicable here: training/testing on labels derived from the received taxonomy risks circularity — Wu & Wang's framing ('semantic boundaries') explicitly asks whether the boundaries the tradition posits are quantitatively real, which is the same construct-validity question our H-C1 addresses; different DH papers reach different conclusions about how sharply the four/six traditions separate.

Coverage caveat (flagged, not contested): OpenAlex was rate-limited (HTTP 429) for part of this session, and its indexing of Chinese-language DH work (e.g., 数字人文 studies of 先秦 texts, the Jin Guantao/Liu Qingfeng quantitative studies of the Lüshi Chunqiu, CTEXT-based projects) is uneven. Item 8's survey is therefore explicitly non-exhaustive; a follow-up sweep of Chinese-language DH venues is recommended before claiming novelty of our design.

payload.objective: H-W1: a reader sealed in 1930 (instrument talkie) already separates what was later called analytic vs continental. H-W2: hindsight gap G > 0 - the modern reader (qwen) separates the later label more sharply than talkie does, beyond qwen's general advantage on labels that already existed in 1930 (H-W2 as pre-registered in list_experiments).

design.step_1_taxonomies: Five rival partitions, one per advocate dispatch, all from the literature with citations: (1) T_retro - the post-1945 analytic/continental partition applied retrospectively to the 25 authors; (2) T_1930 - the partition a well-read person around 1930 would have used (e.g. idealism/realism/pragmatism or national-school schemes from pre-1931 textbooks and surveys); (3) T_lang - confound control: written in English vs translated into English; (4)+(5) two further rivals the advocates find themselves in the literature (candidates: genre/form, national tradition, idealism-vs-rest).
design.step_2_core: hindsight_gap(retro_taxonomy_id=T_retro, contemporary_taxonomy_id=T_1930) - 2 credits, computes its four supporting LOUO scores (T_retro and T_1930 on talkie and qwen) and returns G with bootstrap interval. This is the H-W2 test.
design.step_3_targeted_tournaments: (a) tournament(T_retro, talkie) - 1 credit: permutation p-value/interval for H-W1 proper (is the later partition visible to the sealed reader above its own null?). (b) tournament(T_lang, talkie) - 1 credit: confound control; if language-of-origin predicts placement as well as T_retro, H-W1 is reopened as translation-surface artifact. (c) tournament(T_1930, talkie) - 1 credit: shows whether talkie validates the period-available map at all (baseline; a talkie that scores near null on everything would make H-W1's direction ambiguous).
design.step_4_skeptic: skeptic attacks the result block before any further spend; then candidate_experiments (>=3 candidates with expected_learning/feasibility/cost_credits/mind-changing outcome) + decision entry.
design.budget: 8 credits: hindsight_gap 2 + three tournaments 3 = 5 committed, 3 held for contingency (candidates: a second advocate-rival tournament on talkie to strengthen the comparison set; qwen-side tournament on T_retro if the G interval needs a per-pair p-value; lex instrument check on T_retro if model-based instruments disagree).

decision_rules.H_W1_supported_if: tournament(T_retro, talkie) chance_corrected clearly above its null (permutation p < 0.05) AND T_retro on talkie is not explained by T_lang (T_lang on talkie does not match or exceed it; if it does, H-W1 is reopened as possible translation confound and reported as contested).
decision_rules.H_W1_refuted_if: T_retro on talkie indistinguishable from its own null.
decision_rules.H_W2_supported_if: hindsight_gap G > 0 with bootstrap interval excluding 0.
decision_rules.reporting: Negative/null results reported as results; intervals preserved; contested labels and untestable authors listed. No reopening of line 1 (Chinese corpus) under any outcome.

payload.why_competes_with_T_retro: The analytic/continental split (T_retro) is a post-1945 retrospective projection that lumps Kant, Hegel, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Kierkegaard, Bergson, Croce and Eucken together as 'continental' and splits the English speakers between 'analytic' and 'neither'; T_ideanat instead explains the sorting of the same 25 authors by doctrinal allegiance on the idealism-empiricism/naturalism axis as codified by Passmore (1957) and the revolt-against-idealism literature: it puts the anglophone idealists Green, Bosanquet, Royce (and arguably Whitehead) on the same side as Kant and Hegel, places the pragmatists in their own mediating movement rather than a residual 'neither' class, and separates Nietzsche, Kierkegaard, Bergson and Schopenhauer off a 'philosophy of life' line rather than mere geography - so the two partitions make measurably different predictions about which authors cluster in the corpus.

payload.title: The professionalization divide: professional university philosophy (chairs and specialized academic audiences) vs independent man-of-letters philosophy (outside the university, general educated readership)
payload.source_claim: Institutional-sociological partition drawn from the intellectual-history literature on the professionalization of philosophy c. 1870-1930: Collini, Public Moralists (Oxford UP 1991) on Britain's shift from generalist public moralists (Mill, Spencer) to specialized academic culture (Green, Sidgwick, the Cambridge/Oxford professoriate); Reuben, The Making of the Modern University (Chicago UP 1996) on the professionalization of American philosophy (James, Dewey, Royce); Ringer, The Decline of the German Mandarins (Harvard UP 1969) on the German professorial mandarinate (Kant-Hegel-Eucken lineage) vs anti-academic modernists (Nietzsche, Schopenhauer's heirs); Hollinger, 'The Problem of Pragmatism in American History' (JAH 1980) on pragmatism's academic professional identity and Peirce's marginality. Criterion: did the author work inside the professional university establishment (chair/fellowship, technical disciplinary audience), or as an independent writer for the general educated public?

payload.why_it_competes_with_analytic_continenta: This partition competes with the analytic/continental split (T_retro) because it cross-cuts doctrinal traditions with an institutional fault line that actually sorted these authors in their own era: it places Bergson, Eucken, Mach and Poincare in the SAME class as Russell, Moore and Whitehead (university professionals), while grouping Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Kierkegaard and Croce with Mill, Spencer, Comte, Peirce and Santayana as independents writing for the general reading public - so where T_retro predicts sorting by philosophical doctrine/lineage, this taxonomy predicts sorting by career structure, venue and audience (technical monographs and lecture courses vs essays, periodicals and bestsellers), and the two hypotheses make different predictions especially for the essayistic 'analytic' figures (Russell's popular work) and the professorial 'continental' figures (Bergson, Eucken).
